clue.text: Favourite hedgerow plant' for birds' nests in Limerick

explanation.surface: A naturalist praises a hedgerow plant that birds choose for nesting in an Irish county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limerick' looks like the Irish county; it is the verse form. In Edward Lear's limerick an old man with a beard finds owls, a hen, larks and a wren have all built their nests in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild clematis, common in English hedges, is named for its fluffy grey seed heads; Lear's nonsense verse has birds nesting in an elderly man's whiskers.

explanation.surface: A board game left unplayed in the cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the shelf' looks like storage; it describes an unmarried woman thought past marrying age.
explanation.definitionFit: A card game in which players avoid being left with the odd queen; also a dated term for a spinster, unwed and overlooked.

indicators.note: in places the pole's letter inside the word door

parts.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for the North Pole

explanation.surface: A kind-hearted Polish man who stays at home.
explanation.walkthrough: The page runs 'in door' together as 'indoor'; read as two words, 'in' puts N, for the North Pole, inside DOOR. 'Pole' looks like a Polish person.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is an adjective for a noun: a giver of money or blood is by nature generous.

parts.note: art means skill, as in the art of persuasion
the Orient is the East, so orientated gives E for east
facts are what is real, reality

explanation.surface: Goods made with craft and a realistic outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orientated' gives E because the Orient is the East.
explanation.definitionFit: Objects made by human hands are products of human work, especially of archaeological interest.

clue.text: Shoots up to the' red light

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: pots means shoots, as in pot a rabbit

explanation.surface: Someone fires a gun as far as the traffic signal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns POTS round in this down entry. The printed solution reads STOB, but the last letter is unchecked and both definition and wordplay give a P.
explanation.definitionFit: A red traffic signal tells drivers to halt.

parts.note: Claudius is not the Roman emperor here but Hamlet's uncle, king of Denmark, whose castle the play is set in

explanation.surface: A question of where a Roman emperor held power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Claudius' suggests the Roman emperor; it is the usurping king in Hamlet, set in Denmark.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danish castle at Helsingør is the setting of Shakespeare's Hamlet, in which Claudius is king.

explanation.surface: A customer asks a hat-maker to fill the order again.
explanation.walkthrough: Split with a hyphen, the word is an instruction to put a new cap on, the sort of order a hatter might get.
explanation.definitionFit: A summary going over points again; also, literally, to cover with a cap again, work for a hat-maker.

indicators.note: sounds means the words are said and their sound gives the answer

parts.note: worth a packet means worth plenty of money, cash a lot

explanation.surface: Someone says a whale is very valuable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sounds' signals that 'cash a lot', meaning worth a packet, is said to give the whale's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Another name for the sperm whale, the large toothed whale.

parts.note: read not as low mood but as a physical hollow pressed into a surface

explanation.walkthrough: 'depression' looks like low mood; here it is a hollow pressed into something, as on a car panel.
explanation.definitionFit: Something marked with a hollow or knock, like a bumped car door.

clue.text: Do U.N. members contribute to these?

definitions.text: Do U.N. members contribute to these?

parts.note: the members of the United Nations are countries, that is nations

explanation.surface: A question about whether member states pay into the United Nations' funds.
explanation.definitionFit: Contributions or gifts are what the whole clue describes, and the wordplay spells them as DO plus the countries in the UN.

explanation.surface: A question of which university college a poet attended.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is': the poet John Clare is also a Cambridge college's name.
explanation.definitionFit: John Clare was a nineteenth-century English rural poet, and Clare College is one of the colleges of Cambridge University.

clue.text: Directors helpless as a result of publicity agents' quarrel ?

parts.note: an ad is the product of publicity agents, advertising for short
a rift is a quarrel or breach between people

explanation.surface: A firm's board is left powerless after a row among its publicity men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Directors' are those steering a ship; with no control they drift, so the phrase means cast loose. The answer split as AD RIFT is a quarrel among advertising people.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat floating without power or steering is at the mercy of the current, so those in charge of it are helpless.

clue.text: In the holiday album? It's killing!

definitions.text: In the holiday album? It's killing!

parts.words: In the holiday album? It's killing!
parts.note: a quick informal photo goes in a holiday album, and the same words split in two describe a fast gunshot that kills

explanation.surface: Someone laughs at a hilarious picture in a friend's holiday photo collection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Killing' looks like 'hilarious'; read literally it describes a quick shot fired without careful aim.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal photograph is the typical holiday-album picture, and a snap shot is a hurried shot with a gun.

clue.text: Put down the mighty from his seat, do we infer ?

parts.note: the prefix de- means remove or bring down from
Il Duce, 'the leader', was the title of Mussolini, a mighty dictator

explanation.surface: A line from the Magnificat about toppling the powerful, followed by a question of reasoning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He hath put down the mighty from their seat' is from the Magnificat; removing Il Duce, Mussolini, from power would be to de-Duce him.
explanation.definitionFit: To reason out a conclusion from evidence is to draw it logically, which is what inferring means.

clue.text: Allegedly what Cinna was torn for

definitions.text: Allegedly what Cinna was torn for

parts.words: Allegedly what Cinna was torn for
parts.note: in Julius Caesar the mob mistakes Cinna the poet for a conspirator and cries 'Tear him for his bad verses'

explanation.surface: A question about why a Roman was torn apart.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Act 3, the crowd attacks Cinna the poet; when he protests he is the wrong Cinna they shout 'Tear him for his bad verses!'
explanation.definitionFit: Clumsy, comic or badly written verse, the bad poetry the mob blames.

parts.note: the other entry names a plant with grey fluffy seed heads and an elderly man's whiskers, both streaked with grey

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to the hedgerow plant and the bearded elderly man of the first clue; both are grey-streaked.
explanation.definitionFit: Grey or grey-flecked hair, as on an elderly man's chin, is the usual sense of this word for whiskers.

parts.note: not gas weapons but the lifting gas in airships that raided Britain in the First World War

explanation.walkthrough: 'gas' suggests poison gas attacks; it is the hydrogen keeping German airships aloft as they bombed Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: German rigid airships, named after their designer the Count, bombed British cities in 1915-18.

parts.note: a lift attendant's question answered by a direction straight upward

explanation.surface: A lift attendant asks if you are going up and you say yes, straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'straightway' looks like 'immediately'; read as 'straight way' it is the direction going straight up.
explanation.definitionFit: Upright, at right angles to the horizon, going straight upwards.

clue.text: Got most out of least reading ?

definitions.text: Got most out of least reading

parts.words: Got most out of least reading
parts.note: absorbing something thoroughly is getting most from it, while a condensed summary, a digest, is the least reading

explanation.surface: A question about a student who learnt the most while reading the least.
explanation.walkthrough: A digest is a condensed summary, so to have read only the digest is to read least; the past tense means took in fully.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking in and understanding something fully is to absorb it, as a stomach absorbs food.

parts.note: a lustre, or lustrum, is a period of five years, so two of them added together make a ten-year span

explanation.surface: Age makes something shine all the brighter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lustre' looks like shine; it is also a lustrum, five years, and five plus five years is ten.
explanation.definitionFit: A period of ten years, which two five-year lustres together make.

indicators.note: the letters of the words pest and is, being rearranged, turn into a new word

explanation.surface: A nuisance of a person is acting out of malice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being' signals the rearrangement of PESTIS. The definition is loose: one who spites another is vindictive towards them.
explanation.definitionFit: To act out of spite towards someone is to be malicious and vengeful towards them.

clue.text: Well, son, you need a compress

definitions.text: Well, son, you need a compress

indicators.note: compress means squeeze, so the letters of well and son are squeezed into a new shape

explanation.surface: A parent tells a child with a bump to put a cold pad on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'compress' squeezes WELLSON into a new order; the whole clue also says when a compress is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Puffy and enlarged by injury or inflammation, the state a cold pad treats.

clue.text: Man was given dominion over everything that this

definitions.text: Man was given dominion over everything that this

parts.words: Man was given dominion over everything that this
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Genesis, where man rules over every creeping thing that moves upon the earth

explanation.surface: A half-quoted verse from Genesis on humanity's rule over creation.
explanation.walkthrough: Genesis 1:26 in the King James Bible gives man dominion 'over every creeping thing that ... upon the earth'; the missing word is the archaic verb form.
explanation.definitionFit: The King James wording uses the archaic third-person ending -eth for the verb meaning crawls.

indicators.note: unobvious says the name Dupré is disguised, its letters rearranged out of sight

explanation.surface: A mysterious, unremarkable man named Dupré.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unobvious' disguises DUPRE; the result, French for lost, means hidden from view, so the whole clue is the definition too.
explanation.definitionFit: A word borrowed from French meaning lost or hidden away, out of sight.

parts.note: a direction in a musical score telling players to move smoothly from note to note

explanation.surface: Good advice for someone learning to fly a glider.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like 'reliable', and 'gliding' suggests aircraft; it is music, the instruction to play notes smoothly joined.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian musical term meaning played smoothly, notes flowing on without a break.

parts.note: one is the indefinite article a
one from the nine Muses of Greek myth is a muse

explanation.surface: An offer to entertain someone selected out of nine.
explanation.walkthrough: The nine are the Muses, goddesses of the arts in Greek myth; one of them is a Muse.
explanation.definitionFit: To divert or delight someone is to entertain them.

parts.note: a punning line the poet is said to have written after his secret marriage cost him his post; the blank is his wife's first name

explanation.walkthrough: Donne secretly married Anne More and was dismissed and jailed; he punned 'John Donne, Anne Donne, Un-done'.
explanation.definitionFit: The first name of the poet's wife, Anne More, which the blank needs.

parts.note: lug is informal British slang for an ear

explanation.surface: A gloomy description of how some doctor looks.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic word for gloomy or cheerless, a shortened form of dreary.

parts.note: a single word describing something going on without pause

explanation.definitionFit: Going on without interruption or break is the plain sense of both words.

parts.note: one of the two courtiers at Hamlet's castle, whose name splits into a trade body and a ship's back end

explanation.surface: A portly courtier at the Danish royal court.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is Hamlet's castle. 'Corporation' is old slang for a pot belly, but it also means a guild, and the name ends in STERN, a prominent rear.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosencrantz's companion, a courtier summoned by Claudius in Shakespeare's Hamlet.
